items.title: backlog spec: how should a comment stating a workflow SHAPE or prose ENUMERATION be mechanically checked?
items.eli5: Some source-code comments describe a workflow's shape (e.g. "steps run in this order") or enumerate a fixed list, without naming a specific file/symbol/path. The existing check:comment-code-citations gate (shipped 2026-10-04) only reconciles comments that name a concrete identifier — a shape or enumeration names none, so it is never checked, and the code behind it can drift silently (the entry cites a 2026-08-31 continuityScore header as the motivating case). The backlog entry already states the desired end property, but not the mechanism: there is no existing tool that parses a free-form "shape" or "enumeration" claim and reconciles it against code. Turning this into a concrete, implementable spec (what counts as a checkable shape/enumeration claim, and what tool would check it) is a design call, not a mechanical fix leg 2 can apply on its own.
items.question: Should this stay an open backlog item as-is (no mechanism proposed yet), should it be narrowed to a scoped A→B spec (e.g. "require every workflow-shape comment to cite a sites-pinned test" rather than a general-purpose shape parser), or should it be dropped as not worth mechanizing (rely on doc review to catch drift here)?

options.label: Keep as-is
options.answer: Keep the entry open as currently written; no new mechanism proposed yet, revisit later.

options.label: Narrow to a sites-pinned-citation requirement
options.answer: Narrow the fix to requiring every workflow-shape/enumeration comment to cite a sites-pinned test or spec, rather than building a general shape/enumeration parser.

options.label: Drop — not worth mechanizing
options.answer: Drop this entry; rely on the nightly doc-review pass to catch workflow-shape/enumeration drift by hand rather than building a mechanical check.

items.subject: session-start-guards.mjs's stale-main-behind-origin check reads CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR (the main checkout) instead of the session's own worktree, producing a false "BEHIND origin/main" warning inside a lap worktree that is actually level with origin
items.title: Leg-3 proposal P70: fix session-start-guards.mjs's stale-main check to read the session's own worktree, not CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR
items.eli5: When you work inside a git worktree (a second checkout linked to the same repo, used for a "lap" of work), the SessionStart hook that warns "you are behind origin/main, sync before writing code" was checking the MAIN checkout's git state, not the worktree you are actually sitting in. So a worktree that was perfectly up to date with origin/main still got the scary warning, because the separate main checkout happened to be stale. This exact bug (and an identical one in a different hook, the commit-time merge-routing check) was already logged as two separate backlog entries on two different dates (2026-10-06 and 2026-10-09), which is the nightly routine's bar for calling something a genuine recurring pattern rather than a one-off. Tonight's leg-3 pass wrote a ready-to-apply patch for the smaller of the two bugs: it adds a small helper that trusts the session's own working directory (the same pattern a few lines below in the same file already uses for a different check) and falls back to the old behavior whenever that information is not available, so nothing regresses for a session that is not in a worktree. A failing regression test was run against the unfixed code first (red), then against the patched code (green), and the existing test suite for this file still passes. The second bug (same root cause, in the commit-time merge-routing check) needs a different, larger fix and was deliberately left as a named follow-up rather than folded into tonight's patch.
items.question: Apply the P70 proposal (fix session-start-guards.mjs's stale-main check to read the session worktree instead of the main checkout) as written, and separately decide whether to also scope a fix for the related pre-commit-gate.mjs incomingPaths bug (2026-10-09, left out of this proposal as a materially different, larger change)?

options.label: Apply as-is
options.answer: Land the P70 patch (session-start-guards.mjs fix + regression test) as proposed; track the pre-commit-gate.mjs incomingPaths bug separately.

options.label: Apply, and also scope the pre-commit-gate.mjs follow-up now
options.answer: Land the P70 patch now, and additionally open a scoped task this lap to extend gitTargetDir's parsing to track a leading `cd` in a compound command, fixing the 2026-10-09 sibling bug.

options.label: Hold — needs more review
options.answer: Do not apply yet; the patch needs further review before landing.

items.subject: The weekly /insights pass suggests always committing completed green work before ending a turn (and checkpoint-committing each lap item rather than batching to closeout), which conflicts with this harness's own Git Safety Protocol instruction to never commit unless explicitly asked
items.title: Insights suggestion: adopt an auto-commit-on-green policy for laps, despite the harness's "only commit when asked" default?
items.eli5: The weekly usage-insights report (built from 406 of your Claude Code sessions) noticed that long autonomous laps sometimes end with finished, test-passing work left uncommitted, because a session stops rather than committing without being asked — and then a usage or spend limit kills the session before anyone commits it, so the work is lost or has to be redone. Its suggested fix is to add a rule telling Claude to always commit completed green work, and to commit after each individual backlog item rather than saving everything for the end. The problem is that this directly contradicts an existing, more fundamental rule every session already follows: "NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to." That rule exists on purpose, to stop an agent from making git history changes you did not approve. So this is not a free fix — it is a real tradeoff between losing uncommitted work on a crash versus an agent committing things you have not reviewed. A middle path (e.g. auto-commit only inside a lap the owner has already told the agent to run autonomously, or only to a disposable branch/worktree, or only with a stated justification each time) is possible but is itself a policy call, not something that can be inferred from the conflict alone.
items.question: Should a lap be allowed to auto-commit completed, green, test-passing work without being asked each time (optionally scoped to e.g. explicitly-autonomous laps, or worktree branches only), overriding the general "only commit when asked" rule in that scope — or should the existing rule stand as-is, accepting that an interrupted lap can lose uncommitted work?

options.label: Allow auto-commit, scoped to autonomous laps
options.answer: Add a scoped exception: inside an explicitly autonomous lap (e.g. a nightly run or a lap the owner told the agent to run end-to-end), commit each backlog item once it reaches a green gate, without asking each time. Ordinary interactive sessions keep the existing "only commit when asked" rule.

options.label: Keep the existing rule as-is
options.answer: Do not add an auto-commit exception. Accept that an interrupted lap can lose uncommitted green work; recovering it is the cost of keeping every commit explicitly owner-approved.

options.label: Something else
options.answer: Neither option as stated; the owner will specify a different scoping.

evidence: docs/reviews/insights-triage-2026-10-28.md, "Debatable" section items 1, 4 and 5 — the suggestion text, the conflicting Git Safety Protocol rule it was checked against, and why items 4/5 are the same decision restated.

This session's own system instructions state: "NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked" — verified present in the harness-level Git Safety Protocol this run operates under.

items.subject: The weekly /insights pass suggests cancelling any dispatched worker lane idle or reasoning-only for more than 10 minutes, but that specific numeric threshold conflicts with the documented rule that a cap or timeout must come from a measurement, never from feel
items.title: Insights suggestion: adopt a >10-minute idle-timeout for stalled dispatch lanes, or derive the threshold from measurement instead?
items.eli5: The weekly usage-insights report noticed that dispatched worker lanes (sub-agents handed a task) sometimes get stuck — one example cost about 30 minutes producing nothing but reasoning before anyone noticed and cancelled it. Its suggested fix is a rule: automatically cancel and retry any lane idle (or stuck only "thinking") for more than 10 minutes. The owner has a standing, explicit rule that a cap or timeout must never be picked "from feel" — it has to come from an actual measurement of real task durations, or it gets removed if nobody can justify the number. "10 minutes" in the suggestion is not measured from anything; it is a round number a report-writer picked. The underlying problem (stalled lanes going unnoticed) is real and already partly addressed by a different practice (reading the "Worker activity" / last-output-timestamp line before deciding to cancel a job), which does not require a fixed timeout at all.
items.question: Should a numeric idle/stall timeout be added for dispatched worker lanes (and if so, what real measurement should set its value), or should the existing practice — read the job's activity/last-output signal and judge per task rather than enforcing one fixed number — stand as the answer to stalled lanes?

options.label: Measure first, then set a threshold
options.answer: Before adopting any numeric idle timeout, gather real stall-duration data from past dispatched jobs (e.g. from the spend/dispatch logs) and derive the threshold from that distribution rather than from the report's round number.

options.label: No fixed timeout — keep the activity-signal practice
options.answer: Reject a fixed idle-timeout; keep relying on the per-job "Worker activity" / last-output-timestamp signal and a human or agent judgment call each time, consistent with "default to no limit."

options.label: Something else
options.answer: Neither option as stated; the owner will specify a different approach.

evidence: docs/reviews/insights-triage-2026-10-28.md, "Debatable" section items 2 and 3 — the suggestion text and the specific threshold objection.

C:\Users\ethan\.claude\CLAUDE.md: "Never set a cap, timeout, retry count or threshold from feel. Default to no limit. A limit you need takes its value from a measurement or a documented upstream constraint. Asked \"why N?\" with no measurement behind N: say so, and remove N." — verified present in this session's global instructions.
The dispatch skill's existing guidance already reads "Read a running job's Worker activity line before you cancel it," which is a judgment-based alternative to a fixed timeout.

premise_probes.contains: "Sub-agent / Dispatch Rules" — cancel any lane idle >10 minutes.
